# Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis

Yongjian Tang¹², Costel Moraru¹, Doruk Tuncel¹, Hanya Elhashemy¹,
Steffen Klepke¹, Thomas Runkler¹² Affiliation: ¹Siemens Research (RPD),
Munich, Germany  
²Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany

###### Abstract

API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software
development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code
generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language
Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code,
existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event – overlooking
the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and
market-driven evolution of these artifacts. To address this issue, we
present Agent4Spec, an autonomous multi-agent framework featuring two
distinct pipelines: (1) a validation pipeline that detects and
self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and (2) a market analysis pipeline
that conducts competitive research, identifies functional gaps against
industry leaders, and automatically generates missing API-spec
functionalities. We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets of API
specifications spanning both general-purpose and industrial scenarios.
Among 9 SOTA LLMs, the top-performer achieves 100% syntax error
detection rates and over 95% implementation success for proposed
corrections, while securing over 50% adoption rates for suggested
endpoint improvements, representing a practical tool for API
development.

###### Index Terms: 

LLMs, agents, software engineering, APIs

## I Introduction

API specifications define the operational contract between service
providers and consumers. For REST services, OpenAPI Specification (OAS)
documents describe endpoints, parameters, schemas, and error cases in a
machine-readable form. Such specifications support client integration,
API testing, and long-term maintenance, while inaccurate or incomplete
specifications can mislead developers and propagate failures across
downstream tools. As software ecosystems evolve, maintaining both the
syntactic validity and practical relevance of these specifications
becomes increasingly difficult.

Recent work has made substantial progress in generating API
specifications from source code \[[9](#bib.bib9), [5](#bib.bib5),
[28](#bib.bib28), [8](#bib.bib8)\] and online documentation
\[[7](#bib.bib7), [6](#bib.bib6)\]. Other studies have examined LLMs for
API documentation understanding and updates \[[3](#bib.bib3),
[4](#bib.bib4), [29](#bib.bib29), [2](#bib.bib2)\]. However, these
efforts mainly target initial specification construction or
document-level maintenance. They provide limited support for the
post-generation stage, where developers must validate full OAS files,
implement repairs safely, and decide whether the API should evolve to
match current market expectations.

To address this gap, we present Agent4Spec, a multi-agent system for
post-stage API specification validation and enhancement. As shown in
Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis"),
Agent4Spec uses an orchestrator agent to route developer requests into
two task-specific pipelines. The validation pipeline detects OAS syntax
errors and proposes corrections through tool-assisted checking. The
market analysis pipeline identifies the API domain, searches for
competing services and current trends, analyzes functional gaps, and
suggests endpoint-level improvements. A revision agent can then apply
approved changes to the original specification, with optional human
review before market-driven changes are implemented.

![Refer to caption](2610.13273v1/figures/agent4spec_overview_no_bar.png)

Fig. 1: Agent4Spec consists of four core components: an orchestrator
agent $`A_{o}`$ acting as the central controller and communicator; a
validation agent $`A_{v}`$ to detect and resolve specification syntax
errors; multiple sequential agents $`A_{d},A_{m},A_{g},A_{e}`$ to
explore current technology trends and identify gaps against market
leaders for improvement; and finally a revision agent $`A_{r}`$ that
automatically updates specifications based on developer-approved
suggestions.

We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets, Guru-Spec and
Industry-Spec, covering both general-purpose and industrial API
scenarios. The experiments include nine LLMs across proprietary frontier
and compact open-weight tiers, allowing us to study both effectiveness
and resource trade-offs. Our main contributions can be summarized as
follows:

- (i)
  We formulate API specification enhancement as a post-generation
  workflow that jointly considers syntax validation, market analysis,
  and specification revision.
- (ii)
  We propose Agent4Spec, a multi-agent framework that coordinates
  specialized agents for validation, competitive analysis, endpoint
  suggestion, and optional human-approved revision.
- (iii)
  We construct two evaluation datasets, Guru-Spec and Industry-Spec, to
  measure Agent4Spec across general-purpose and industrial API
  specifications.
- (iv)
  We conduct an extensive evaluation across 9 LLMs. The strongest
  frontier models achieve 100% syntax-error detection, over 95% correct
  implementation for proposed corrections, and up to 1.82 human-approved
  endpoint suggestions out of three, while the same evaluation also
  exposes practical limitations of compact models in tool use, full-file
  revision, and market-oriented analysis.

## II Related Work

### II-A API Specification Generation

API specification generation has been studied from both implementation
artifacts and public documentation. For source-code-based generation,
Respector \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] uses static and symbolic program analysis
to infer endpoint methods, parameters, responses, and constraints from
REST API implementations. Recent LLM-based approaches extend this
direction: LRASGen \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] generates RESTful API
specifications from cleaned source code, while OOPS \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]
models cross-file API dependencies and applies self-refinement to
improve OpenAPI Specification (OAS) compliance. In parallel,
documentation-based systems such as SpeCrawler \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] and
OASBuilder \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] generate OAS files from online API
documentation through scraping and LLM-based synthesis. These methods
reduce the cost of producing initial specifications, but they mainly
assume a specific generation setting. Agent4Spec instead targets the
post-generation stage, where an existing OAS file must be validated,
repaired, and potentially enhanced.

### II-B API Documentation Understanding and Maintenance

Several studies examine whether LLMs can understand or update API
documentation. Li et al. \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] evaluate LLM accuracy in API
documentation understanding across programming languages, and Chen et
al. \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] study retrieval-augmented API documentation for
code generation. Lee et al. \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] move closer to
maintenance by extracting API change rules from repository histories and
prompting LLMs to update documentation snippets. These works show that
LLMs can support API-documentation tasks, but they focus on textual
documentation or downstream code assistance. In comparison, Agent4Spec
focuses on machine-readable OAS artifacts and couples validation reports
with full-specification revision.

### II-C Agentic Workflows and Evaluation

LLM-based agentic systems have been widely applied to complex software
engineering tasks \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. ChatDev \[[11](#bib.bib11)\],
Agent4RE \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], and MetaGPT \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] organize
multiple agents into role-based software-development workflows, while
SWE-agent \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], Agent4cs \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], and
AutoCodeRover \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] focus on repository-level issue
resolution and program improvement. These systems demonstrate the value
of task decomposition, tool use, and iterative feedback for software
development. However, they mainly operate on source code, repositories,
or natural-language development tasks. We propose Agent4Spec to target
machine-readable OAS maintenance, where the output must remain
syntactically valid, structurally consistent, and controllable by
developers before endpoint-level changes are applied.

## III Agent4Spec

As illustrated in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis"),
Agent4Spec starts with an orchestrator agent $`A_{o}`$, which serves as
the central coordinator – interacting with the developers while
controlling over all other specialized sub-agents. Once an API
specification $`S_{0}`$ is received, the orchestrator directs the
workflow based on the user’s query – either triggering the validation
agent to detect syntax errors in the document, or forwarding it to a
series of market research agents to identify current technology trends
and leading API service competitors. Notably, only one of these two
pathways is executed before calling the revision agent, ensuring that
the system is not overwhelmed with excessive revision instructions.
Optionally, human developers can be incorporated into this workflow
before the revision agent is triggered, reviewing and selectively
approving the suggestions produced by either the validation or market
analysis pipelines.

### III-A Validation Pipeline

We equip the validation agent with a file reading tool $`T_{r}`$ and an
OpenAPI specification validation tool $`T_{v}`$. Given a local file
path, $`T_{r}`$ enables the agent to thoroughly parse and examine the
uploaded API YAML file in detail, while $`T_{v}`$ utilizes the Python
library openapi_spec_validator to execute the parsed YAML file and
detect whether any syntax errors exist. Based on the resulting error
message, the validation agent proposes fixing solutions to resolve the
identified issues. Using the notation in Table
[I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-A Validation Pipeline ‣ III Agent4Spec ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis"),
the agent output can be defined as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       R_{v}=A_{v}(T_{v}(T_{r}(S_{0}))).
       ```                                |     | (1) |

In the next step, the revision agent can be invoked to implement the
proposed solutions automatically.

| Notation               | Description / Functional Definition                                              |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $`S_{0}`$              | Original OpenAPI specification provided by the user                              |
| $`S_{f}`$              | Final revised OpenAPI specification                                              |
| $`R_{v}`$              | Report of validation errors with proposed correction suggestions                 |
| $`R_{d}`$              | Identified API domain and domain summary                                         |
| $`R_{m}`$              | Synthesized market analysis report                                               |
| $`R_{g}`$              | Gap analysis report with prioritized suggestions                                 |
| $`R_{e}`$              | Endpoint-level report highlighting improvement suggestions                       |
| $`R`$                  | Intermediate report from the validation pipeline or the market analysis pipeline |
| $`R^{\prime}`$         | Revisions approved by human developers in the pipeline report                    |
| $`T_{r}(S)`$           | File Reading Tool: Parses and loads an OpenAPI specification                     |
| $`T_{v}(S)`$           | Validation Tool: Checks OpenAPI compliance and detects syntax errors             |
| $`T_{s}(R_{d})`$       | Web Search Tool: Retrieves market information for API domain $`R_{d}`$           |
| $`A_{o}(S_{0})`$       | Orchestrator Agent: Routes workflow execution and coordinates agents             |
| $`A_{v}(S_{0})`$       | Validation Agent: Suggest corrections from validation errors                     |
| $`A_{d}(S_{0})`$       | Domain Identification Agent: Determines API domain and key characteristics       |
| $`A_{m}(R_{d})`$       | Market Analysis Agent: Searches and synthesizes collected market information     |
| $`A_{g}(R_{m},S_{0})`$ | Gap Analysis Agent: Identifies the gap between our API service & market leaders  |
| $`A_{e}(R_{g},S_{0})`$ | Endpoint Suggestion Agent: Generates endpoint-level improvement proposals        |
| $`A_{r}(R,S_{0})`$     | Revision Agent: Revises the specification using approved suggestions             |

TABLE I: Notation used in Agent4Spec.

### III-B Market Analysis Pipeline

Alternative to syntax validation, orchestrator can also initiate a
market analysis pipeline upon user requests, which consists of four
sequential agents.

1.  1.  Domain Identification Agent: The first agent $`A_{d}`$ reads through
        the uploaded API specification, determines the API domain, and
        summarizes its key developments as bullet points:

    |     |     |     |     |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    |     |

           ``` math
           R_{d}=A_{d}(T_{r}(S_{0})).
           ```                         |     | (2) |

2.  2.  Online Search Agent: The following agent $`A_{m}`$ conducts
        comprehensive market analysis by leveraging an online search tool
        $`T_{s}`$. Given the specified API domain, it formulates search
        queries, executes online web searches, and selects maximum 3 results
        per query, prioritizing authoritative sources such as vendor
        documentation and reputable technology media. Together with the
        browsed website links, the agent synthesizes all retrieved
        information into a market summary:

    |     |     |     |     |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    |     |

           ``` math
           R_{m}=A_{m}(T_{s}(R_{d})),
           ```                         |     | (3) |

    which delivers structured insights on market leaders, landscape,
    emerging trends, and pricing models with quantified statistics where
    available.

3.  3.  Gap Analysis Agent: The gap analysis agent $`A_{g}`$ compares the
        user’s API service against the identified market leaders in
        $`R_{m}`$:

    |     |     |     |     |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    |     |

           ``` math
           R_{g}=A_{g}(R_{m},T_{r}(S_{0})).
           ```                               |     | (4) |

    For each uploaded specification $`S_{0}`$, it highlights missing
    functionalities, design inconsistencies, ecosystem limitations, and
    potential competitive disadvantages. Findings are categorized into
    high-, medium-, and low-priority recommendations accompanied by
    technical impact assessments.

4.  4.  Endpoint Suggestion Agent: The endpoint suggestion agent $`A_{e}`$
        generates concrete API endpoints to address the prioritized gaps:

    |     |     |     |     |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    |     |

           ``` math
           R_{e}=A_{e}(R_{g},T_{r}(S_{0})),
           ```                               |     | (5) |

    which contains endpoint-level enhancements, API schemas, migration
    guidance, along with summarized market insights.

### III-C Specification Revision Agent

Given either validation reports $`R_{v}`$ or market-oriented endpoints
suggestion $`R_{e}`$ from previous agents, the revision agent $`A_{r}`$
implements the corrections to specification $`S_{0}`$ while preserving
its content structure. Furthermore, we develop an iterative
re-validation mechanism to improve the accuracy in large specifications,
where the revised documents are repeatedly sent back to the validation
agent for $`n`$ rounds until all errors are eliminated. Formally, the
final specification $`S_{f}`$ is:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \begin{gathered}S_{f}=A_{r}^{(n)}(R,T_{r}(S_{0})),\\[4.30554pt]
       \scalebox{0.95}{$R=\begin{cases}R_{v},&\text{validation mode}\\
       R_{e},&\text{market analysis mode}\end{cases}$}.\end{gathered}
       ```                                                              |     | (6) |

Once completed, the agent saves the corrected specification locally with
appropriate file naming, and transfers control back to the orchestrator,
ensuring seamless workflow integration within the system.

### III-D Human-in-the-Loop

Based on the improvement suggestions from the two pipelines, human
developers can optionally be involved to review and approve these
recommendations before handing over to the revision agent. The finalized
report, after human approval, can be represented as $`R^{\prime}=H(R)`$.
This step allows flexible quality control in practice and embeds expert
feedback into critical decision-making processes.

## IV Experimental Setup

### IV-A Datasets

To evaluate Agent4Spec across both general-purpose and industrial API
ecosystems, we have curated two datasets of OpenAPI specifications with
complementary features: 1) Guru-Spec contains 300 publicly available API
specifications collected from APIs.guru \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], covering
diverse domains such as cloud services, finance, e-commerce, and
transportation. 2) In contrast, Industry-Spec focuses on 200 industrial
APIs obtained from Xcelerator Developer \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. These APIs
target industrial applications and enterprise services, covering domains
such as automation, Internet of Things, asset management, and
manufacturing. Together, these two datasets enable evaluation across
both broad web services and industrial scenarios. Detailed statistics
are presented in Table
[II](#S4.T2 "TABLE II ‣ IV-A Datasets ‣ IV Experimental Setup ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis").

| Statistic                       | Guru-Spec       | Industry-Spec   |
| ------------------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Number of specifications        | $`300`$         | $`200`$         |
| Total dataset tokens            | $`3\,483\,222`$ | $`1\,684\,932`$ |
| Maximum tokens in a single spec | $`59\,836`$     | $`36\,145`$     |
| Average tokens per spec         | $`11\,610.7`$   | $`8424.7`$      |
| Average lines per spec          | $`1549.2`$      | $`934.4`$       |

TABLE II: Statistics of the curated datasets.

### IV-B Models

We strategically select 9 LLMs that span different performance tiers, as
presented in Table
[III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ IV-B Models ‣ IV Experimental Setup ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis").
We deploy 5 frontier models via APIs, including Claude-Sonnet-4.6
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\] from Anthropic, Gemini-3.1-Pro \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]
from Google, and GPT-5.2, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o \[[21](#bib.bib21),
[20](#bib.bib20), [19](#bib.bib19)\] from OpenAI, which represent the
forefront of LLM capabilities. To complement these proprietary models,
we incorporate four open-source alternatives that ensure reproducibility
and broader applicability: Ministral3-8B \[[26](#bib.bib26)\],
LLaMA3.1-8B \[[25](#bib.bib25)\] from Meta, Qwen3.5-9B
\[[24](#bib.bib24)\] from Alibaba, and Gemma4-4B \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]
from Google. Large-scale language models are accessed through API
gateways, while compact models are deployed via the open-source Ollama
framework, with the temperature parameter of all models set to the
minimal value.

### IV-C Metrics

We select an extensive set of evaluation metrics tailored to each task.
For syntax validation – a task with verifiable outputs, we use
quantitative metrics, including 1) error detection rate (the percentage
of errors identified by the system), 2) solution proposal rate (the
percentage of detected errors for which solutions are proposed), 3)
solution correctness (the percentage of proposed solutions that are
accurate). For API specification revision, we employ 1) correct
implementation rate (the percentage of solutions that are properly
implemented), and 2) successful save rate (the percentage of solutions
locally saved).

Regarding market analysis, where no groundtruth answers are available,
we apply LLM-as-a-judge \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] complemented by human
evaluation. To be more specific, 1) LLM-as-a-judge employs prompt-based
assessment, with grades assigned on a scale from 1 to 5. Given the
empirical evidence that smaller LLMs often struggle in judging summary
quality and even the best one frequently misjudges \[[16](#bib.bib16)\],
we only employ the most competent large-scale models –
Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and GPT-5.2. In comparison, 2) human
evaluation verifies the consistency of LLM-as-a-judge. Three software
developers assess summaries independently on a scale from 1 to 5, with
final scores averaged for fairness. We selected human evaluators based
on their software development experience, code-review skills, and
relevant domain expertise. Finally, we chose two senior software
engineers, each with three years of development experience, and one
junior software developer in industry. In addition to their own
experience and judgment criteria, we also provided the prompt and
grading schema used in LLM-as-a-judge to ensure consistent evaluation.
An example judge prompt to evaluate the quality of market analysis is
demonstrated below:

## V Experiments – Syntax Validation Pipeline

Following the architecture in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis"),
we first evaluate the validation pipeline based on the quantitative
metrics defined in Section
[IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C Metrics ‣ IV Experimental Setup ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis").
For each collected API specification, we manually inject a syntax error
to assess the system’s performance, including invalid data types,
missing parameters, and inconsistent naming. Representative examples of

### V-A Syntax Error Detection

Table
[IV](#S6.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ VI-A Domain Identification ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
compares Agent4Spec with a single-prompt baseline, where the same LLM is
asked to handle validation in one prompt. Across all evaluated models
and datasets, Agent4Spec outperformed the baseline in error detection,
solution proposal, and solution correctness. When $`T_{v}`$ was invoked
reliably, Agent4Spec detected nearly all syntax errors:
Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Gemini-3.1-Pro reached 100.0% detection on both
datasets, while GPT-5.2 and GPT-4.1 remained above 99.0%. GPT-4o was
slightly lower, but still detected 96.0% of errors on Guru-Spec and
94.5% on Industry-Spec. The system proposed a repair for every error it
detected, as reflected in the identical percentages for detected errors
and proposed solutions. Regarding the correctness of solutions, frontier
models achieved 91.5–99.5% correctness, while Qwen-3.5-9B and
Ministral-3-8B dropped to 87.0% and 87.5% on Industry-Spec. The other
two compact models LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-4-4B showed a typical failure
mode: they often stated that they would use $`T_{v}`$ but failed to
activate it, yielding detection rates and correct-solution rates no
higher than 8.0%.

### V-B Syntax Error Revision

Table
[V](#S6.T5 "TABLE V ‣ VI-A Domain Identification ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
evaluates whether the single-prompt baseline and Agent4Spec can
implement the proposed fixes and save a complete revised specification
in its first attempt. This task is more demanding than syntax-error
detection because the revision agent must modify the full API
specification file while preserving its original structure. Compared
with the baseline, Agent4Spec generally achieved higher
correct-implementation and save rates. Large-scale frontier models saved
almost all revised specifications, with Claude-Sonnet-4.6,
Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.2, and GPT-4.1 reaching 100.0% save rates on both
datasets. Their correct-implementation rates were lower, ranging from
82.0% to 98.3% on Guru-Spec and from 73.5% to 98.5% on Industry-Spec.
This gap shows that saving and correctness are separate tool functions:
an agent may save a revised specification even when the implemented
solution is incorrect. In comparison, compact open-weight models
struggled in the full-spec revision setting. Qwen-3.5-9B achieved only
10.3% and 5.5% correct implementation on Guru-Spec and Industry-Spec,
while Ministral-3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Gemma-4-4B were close to zero.
These results indicate that full-specification revision remains
challenging for smaller models. Iterative re-validation after each
revision attempt is necessary to verify the quality of generated API
specifications.

## VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline

Alternatively, the market analysis pipeline can be initiated. Since no
standard answers exist for such open-ended tasks, we employ
LLM-as-a-judge alongside human evaluation.

### VI-A Domain Identification

As the initial step of the market analysis pipeline, domain
identification requires the agent to infer the API scope and summarize
relevant developments.

Figure
[2](#S6.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ VI-A Domain Identification ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
shows that this task is comparatively tractable, with human scores
ranging from 2.76 to 3.82 on the 5-point scale. The highest human-rated
outputs are produced by Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and GPT-5.2,
which receive scores of 3.82, 3.72, and 3.52, respectively. In contrast,
LLM-as-a-judge scores are more conservative and less aligned with the
human ranking. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 assigns particularly strict scores,
mostly between 1.54 and 2.60, while Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.2 provide
intermediate ratings. Despite different scoring behaviors, both
evaluations exhibit a consistent pattern: larger, more recent LLMs
perform better, as evident in the upward trend.

### VI-B Online Search

Figure
[3](#S6.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ VI-B Online Search ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
evaluates the online search stage, where agents must retrieve external
information and synthesize it into market-oriented insights. Compared
with domain identification, this stage produces clearer separation among
models. All three LLM judges rank GPT-5.2 as the strongest performer,
assigning it the highest scores in their respective evaluations (2.66
from Claude-Sonnet-4.6, 2.62 from GPT-5.2, and 3.56 from
Gemini-3.1-Pro). Human evaluators instead rate Claude-Sonnet-4.6 highest
at 3.34, followed by GPT-5.2, Qwen-3.5-9B, and Gemini-3.1-Pro with
closely matched scores of 3.26, 3.24, and 3.18. This pattern indicates
that stronger models generally produce more useful search summaries.

Fig. 3: Evaluation on online search.

Compact models tend to underutilize the search tool, generating market
insights primarily based on their prior knowledge rather than the found
data. While such reports remain readable for human developers, they lack
timely information – a critical shortcoming for market analysis. In
particular, Qwen-3.5-9B appears competitive under human evaluation
despite receiving lower scores from the LLM judges.

### VI-C Gap Analysis

Gap analysis places higher demands on reasoning because the agent must
compare the target API with market alternatives and identify actionable
functional gaps.

Fig. 4: Evaluation on gap analysis.

Figure
[4](#S6.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ VI-C Gap Analysis ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
shows a clear advantage for frontier models, although the exact ranking
varies by evaluator. Human evaluators rate Claude-Sonnet-4.6 highest at
4.74, followed by GPT-4.1 at 4.48 and both GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3.1-Pro at
4.36. Gemini-3.1-Pro as judge assigns similarly high scores to the
frontier group, with Claude-Sonnet-4.6, GPT-5.2, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and
GPT-4.1 all scoring above 4.70. By contrast, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 is
substantially more conservative as an evaluator, assigning no model
above 2.10. GPT-5.2 shows a self-preference pattern, giving its own
output the highest score of 4.02, compared with 3.26 for GPT-4.1 and
3.04 for Claude-Sonnet-4.6. Compact models remain weaker overall,
especially LLaMA-3.1-8B, which receives near-minimal scores from LLM
judges and only 1.82 from human evaluators. This weakness is consistent
with the online-search results: when compact models underuse retrieved
evidence and rely more on prior knowledge, the downstream gap analysis
has a weaker factual basis and performance degrades.

### VI-D Endpoint Suggestion

Endpoint suggestion is the final and most prescriptive stage, requiring
the agent to convert market evidence and gap-analysis findings into
concrete API changes.

Fig. 5: Evaluation on endpoint suggestion.

Figure
[5](#S6.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ VI-D Endpoint Suggestion ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
shows that this requirement separates models more sharply than earlier
stages. Human evaluators rate GPT-4.1 highest at 4.56, followed by
Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at 4.44 and Gemini-3.1-Pro at 3.94. Gemini-3.1-Pro as
judge gives the highest score 4.96 to Claude-Sonnet-4.6, followed by
GPT-4.1 (4.66), Gemini-3.1-Pro (4.64), and GPT-4o (4.52). GPT-5.2
underperforms relative to the strongest frontier models, receiving 3.46
from Gemini-3.1-Pro as judge and 3.04 from both GPT-5.2 and human
evaluators. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 remains conservative as a judge, assigning
all models scores between 1.02 and 1.58. Qwen-3.5-9B also drops sharply,
with a human score of 1.82 despite its competitive online-search score.
Qualitative inspection suggests that GPT-5.2 and Qwen-3.5-9B often
prioritize the generation of market insights report and ignore the
request of endpoints improvement, leading to significantly biased
results and lower scores. Their outputs are therefore informative but
less aligned with this stage’s core target.

### VI-E Human-in-the-Loop

We further evaluate the human-in-the-loop mode in the market analysis
pipeline. Each agent is instructed to provide market insights along with
three endpoint suggestions, and human developers record how many
suggestions they would approve for specification revision. Figure
[6](#S6.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ VI-E Human-in-the-Loop ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
reports the average number of approved suggestions out of three. For
Agent4Spec, proprietary models substantially outperform compact
open-weight models, with GPT-5.2 achieving the highest acceptance score
of 1.82 out of 3, followed closely by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (1.79),
Gemini-3.1-Pro (1.73), and GPT-4.1 (1.71). GPT-4o remains lower at 1.48,
but still exceeds all compact models. Among compact models, Qwen-3.5-9B
and Ministral-3-8B achieve 0.78 and 0.74 accepted suggestions, while
Gemma-4-4B and LLaMA-3.1-8B remain near 0.33. These results indicate
that stronger tool use and reasoning improve endpoint-suggestion
quality. However, even the best model averages fewer than two accepted
suggestions, highlighting the value of human review before applying
market-driven API changes in practice.

Fig. 6: Endpoint suggestions approved by humans.

### VI-F Resource Consumption

Figure
[7](#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-F Resource Consumption ‣ VI Experiments – Market Analysis Pipeline ‣ Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis")
reports the average output-token usage and inference latency per API
specification under our experimental deployment. Compact open-weight
models are served locally with Ollama on a single Apple M4 Pro machine
with a 12-core CPU, 16-core GPU. Frontier models are accessed through
API gateways, and all models use the minimum temperature setting.
Because the input length is largely determined by the API specification
itself, output tokens provide a clearer measure of model-side generation
cost. Syntax validation is consistently more efficient than online
search. Across models, validation consumes 162–1,402 output tokens,
whereas online search requires 720–5,467 output tokens, due to its
four-stage design and tool-assisted web searches. The same pattern
appears in latency: validation completes in 1.8–37.1 seconds, while
online search takes 16.1–182.2 seconds. Locally deployed compact models
are especially latency-bound, with Ministral-3-8B and Qwen-3.5-9B
requiring 173.2 and 182.2 seconds for online search respectively.
Gemma-4-4B and LLaMA-3.1-8B take less time since they may fail to invoke
the tools and directly end the session. In contrast, API-based frontier
models complete online search much faster, ranging from 16.1 seconds for
GPT-4.1 to 36.0 seconds for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 produces
the longest online-search outputs (5,467 tokens), but its API latency
remains moderate at 18.9 seconds. These results show that model
deployment mode and task complexity jointly determine the resource
consumption.

Fig. 7: Agent4Spec token consumption and inference latency per API
specification across different LLMs.

## VII Conclusions and Future Work

This paper presents Agent4Spec, a multi-agent framework that supports
both technical validation and market-driven improvement of OpenAPI
specifications. Experiments on Guru-Spec and Industry-Spec datasets show
that the framework is highly effective when paired with frontier LLMs.
Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Gemini-3.1-Pro achieve complete syntax-error
detection on both datasets, while other frontier models remain close to
this level. The results also show that full-specification revision is
more difficult than error diagnosis, since successful file generation
does not always imply a correct repair. For market-driven improvement,
we observe similar patterns, where larger models produce more relevant
and timely outputs across the four sequential stages. Human evaluation
further confirms the practical value of the suggested API endpoints.
Resource measurements show that task complexity and deployment mode
jointly determine cost: market analysis is token-intensive, while
locally deployed compact models require long inference latency. Overall,
Agent4Spec shows that LLM agents can advance API maintenance beyond
static validation, but reliable deployment still depends on model
capability, tool usage, verification, and human oversight.

Future work should extend experiments to more emerging models to
generalize the observed trade-offs in accuracy, token cost, and latency.
Furthermore, exploring specialized prompting strategies, supervision
mechanisms, or fine-tuning approaches may improve models’ tool-use
reliability and make local deployment more practical for API maintenance
tasks. Given that no public benchmark is available for OpenAPI
specification repair, our experiments rely on manually injected common
errors, including invalid data types, missing required fields, and
structural inconsistencies. Future work should develop a repair
benchmark from real-world version histories and issue reports, where
faulty and corrected API specifications can be paired directly.
